title: Dolphins: My Close Encounters
excerpt: Swiss biologist uncovers the dirty secrets of the Red Sea dolphins, in this very thoughtful and profound sea documentary - from the 9th El Gouna Film Festival
content:
Swiss biologist uncovers the dirty secrets of the Red Sea dolphins, in this very thoughtful and profound sea documentary - from the 9th El Gouna Film Festival

QUICK’N DIRTY: LIVE FROM EL GOUNA

Angela Ziltener was fascinated by dolphins from her early years, we learn from her childhood drawings. Despite coming from Switzerland – a landlocked nation thousands of miles from the natural environment of such aquatic mammals – she was determined to work with the creatures as soon as she grew. She wanted to do for dolphins what Jane Goodall did for chimpanzees. The late British primatologist pioneered harmonious integration between researcher and animals as early as in the 1960s, raising quite a few eyebrows in the process.

Many scientists believe that nature professionals should keep an emotional distance from the subject of their study. Much like Jane, Angela found that borderline impossible, not least because dolphins are highly intelligent and passionate creatures. She was quickly welcomed into a pod in the Egyptian Red Sea coast. She followed the animals for 15 years, witnessing the birth of the second and the third generation. Her “subjects” had individual names and personalities. Laura is playful. Ferdinand is inquisitive. Magic is a fighter who survived a horrific ordeal and is now witnessing her child go through a remarkably similar tragedy. Angela is able to identify 100s of dolphins through a combination of their demeanour and their dorsal fin (“that’s their fingerprint”, she clarifies).

Most of the m0vie consists of footage captured by Angela and fellow scientist Gemma underwear over the course of the decade and a half in question. These images are interspersed with talking heads interviews with present-day Angela and other marine life experts. Historical footage of dolphins in captivity with multiple wires attached to their heads for the purpose of conducting behavioural tests is disturbing to watch. Angela ascertains that her research is far more relevant precisely because she studies the animals in their natural environment, and that her methods are non-intrusive.

There is very little doubt that these animals trust Angela. They play “ball” with an inflated puffer fish and a turtle, often “passing” the unusual toy to the perplexed scientist. They proudly introduce their calves to their human friend. And they ask Angela for help freeing the fish trapped in underwater cages abandoned by unscrupulous fishers (suggesting that dolphins are capable of empathy). Their sophistication is such that they use coral reef for skin care (a marine beauty spa), and they self-medicate with underwater herbs. They even have their own culture, something hitherto thought to be exclusive to human beings. The findings are groundbreaking, with the news splashing the covers of the scientific magazines worldwide. There are also moments of heartbreak: Magic begs the powerless scientist to save the life of her child; a male dolphin with a severely wounded fin seems aware of his imminent demise. While underwater animals cannot shed tears, film lovers are guaranteed to do so.

The crystal clear images speak for themselves: the interactions are authentic and moving. Still, Angela is very cautious with her conclusions. She admits that – however strong the anecdotal evidence – there is no hard scientific proof of the dolphins’ allegiance towards her. Her attitude is measured and responsible, as she seeks to strike the balance between the professional and the emotional.

The film also contains insight into destructive human practices. Unregulated dolphin tourism can have devastating consequences: hordes of curious dolphin chasers can cause entire populations to abandon an area permanently.

Much like Oscar winner My Octopus Teacher (Pippa Ehrlich and James Reed, 2021), this co-production of the United Kingdom, Egypt and Switzerland opts for a first-person approach, while also proposing that us humans have a lot to learn from our animal friends (much more than the other way around). Both movies succeed in their artistic choices. British documentarist Barny Revill allows Angela to take full control of the narrative. It is her voiceover that guides the story. Revill shuns the poetic and the experimental in favour of the technical, the professional and also the human touch. This creative decision was very fortunate because the movie characters – woman and dolphins – are bursting with charisma. Dolphins: My Close Encounters is a clear, objective, insightful and moving documentary.

Natalie Holt’s gentle music score – with a touch of Wagner’s Tristan and Isolde – also deserves a mention. The arrangements are pervasive however never invasive. Special effects are either absent or barely perceptible, allowing Angela and the sea creatures to reign supreme in their chosen/natural habitat.

Dolphins: My Close Encounters just showed in the Spotlight Screenings section of the 9th El Gouna Film Festival, where this piece was written. The event is held on the coast the Egyptian Red Sea, where the dolphins live. The movie originally premiered at the Zurich Film Festival just a couple of weeks earlier.
